extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic, philosophers, and those studying classification and definition
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the doctrine of the Predicables and the principles of logical classification and definition: genus, species, differentia, proprium, and accidens; when classes are 'real Kinds' and how names/connotation relate to classification. Intended as a textbook-style treatment of these logical concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predicables (fivefold division of General Names)
rubrics_metrics.description: General names, when predicated of a thing, may be of five varieties: genus, species, differentia, proprium, and accidens. These distinctions do not express what the predicate is in its own meaning, but the relation it bears to the subject on the particular occasion of predication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these five categories to analyse how a predicate relates to a subject; remember they are relative terms: the same name may be a genus, species, or differentia depending on the subject. Examples: 'animal' is a genus with respect to man, but a species with respect to Being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus and Species (popular vs. Aristotelian meanings)
rubrics_metrics.description: In popular sense, any two classes one including the other may be called genus and species (e.g., Animal/Man). Aristotelian logicians used a stricter sense: genus and species must be of the 'essence' of the subject — i.e., denote real Kinds distinguished by an indeterminate multitude of properties, not mere accidental differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish whether a class is being used in ordinary/popular classification or in the stricter logical sense. Be cautious: terms like 'biped' might be treated as genus in popular use but not as genus in Aristotelian/rigorous logic if they are not of the subject's essence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for a 'Real Kind' (essence / inexhaustible properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'real Kind' (logical species) is one distinguished from other classes by an indeterminate multitude of properties not derivable from one another; its distinguishing differences are 'inexhaustible' rather than merely finite and determinate (as with color classes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To determine whether a class is a real Kind, ask whether the distinguishing attribute is an index to many other properties (unknown and known) such that recognising the difference is imperative for classification. If the distinguishing differences can be reduced to a finite set derivable from one another, the class may be an accidental or convenience-based division rather than a real Kind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximate (infima) species and hierarchical consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: The proximate (lowest) Kind to which an individual is referable (its infima species) comprehends necessarily the whole of the common properties of every other real Kind to which the individual can be referred; any larger Kind predicable of the individual will be a genus relative to that proximate Kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When fixing the proximate species, its properties will include (known or unknown) properties of higher-level kinds; use the proximate species as the immediate classificatory identity (example: Socrates → proximate Kind 'man').

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentia (specific difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Differentia is the surplus part of the connotation of a species-name beyond what the genus connotes; it is that which, added to the connotation of the genus, completes the connotation of the species. Differentiae need not be unique nor fixed across all classifications — they depend on the principle and purpose of classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the differentia according to the classificatory purpose (ordinary meaning or technical sense). Example: 'rationality' as differentia of man in ordinary use; in a Linnaean technical use, a different set of anatomical traits might be the differentia. Be aware that a species may have different differentiae in different classificatory schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proprium (property necessary but not connoted)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Proprium is an attribute that is not part of the connotation (definition) of the species-name yet follows necessarily from connoted attributes; it is predicated accidentally but necessarily (inseparably attached).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two kinds of Proprium: (1) those that follow by demonstration (logical consequence) — e.g., opposite sides equal in a parallelogram; (2) those that follow by causation — e.g., ability to understand language follows from rationality in man. Use Proprium to record necessary consequences of the connoted attributes even if not definitional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidens (accident) — separable and inseparable
rubrics_metrics.description: Accidens comprises attributes neither connoted by the name nor known to have any necessary connection with connoted attributes. These may be inseparable accidents (universal in the species as far as known but not necessary — e.g., blackness of crows) or separable accidents (not universal or temporally variable — e.g., being born, location, posture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat inseparable accidents as universal in experience but logically removable; treat separable accidents as contingent attributes applying to some individuals or some times. Distinguish accidents from Proprium by checking for any necessary inference from connoted attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unlimited power of framing classes vs. practical conformity to 'Kinds'
rubrics_metrics.description: Any attribute difference gives authority to form a class (names create classes), so the number of possible classes is boundless; yet some class divisions correspond to more radical distinctions in nature (Kinds) while others serve convenience and may be arbitrary depending on purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that classification choices are often guided by practical or scientific convenience; when forming primary divisions, one may legitimately choose demarcations not coinciding with metaphysical 'Kinds' if those choices better serve the classificatory purpose (e.g., dividing animals by warm/cold-blooded for zoological utility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of names, connotation, and classification (technical senses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Names connote attributes; by employing a general name we create a class of things corresponding to that signification. Names may acquire special or technical connotations for scientific classification, which then change what the name connotes in that context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using terms in technical discourse, explicitly note any special connotation assigned (definition). Beware of ambiguity between ordinary and technical uses (example: 'man' connoting rationality ordinarily vs. specific teeth-count in Linnaean taxonomy); if necessary, define the term's technical connotation to avoid confusion.
